growth_story.headline: Tunisia grew steadily for two decades, then stalled after the 2011 revolution; income per person in 2025 was about where it first was in 2014.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2010 income per person grew 3.3 percent a year, helped by an export sector along the coast that ran under lighter rules while the state kept tight control of the home market. The World Bank later wrote that this model rested on barriers to entry and favours for the well connected, and that too few good jobs for graduates and wide gaps between regions fed the January 2011 revolution. Since 2011 growth has averaged 0.3 percent a year: income per person fell 3.1 percent in 2011, rose slowly to a peak in 2019, then fell 9.7 percent in 2020 with the pandemic. The recovery has been slow, with drought and weak demand in 2023, and in 2025 income per person was 1.7 percent below its 2019 peak and about where it first was in 2014. Recent World Bank and EBRD reports point to high public debt, limited access to foreign markets, heavy borrowing at home, a large role for state-owned firms and low investment.

threads.title: Open coast, closed home market
threads.text: From the 1970s Tunisia ran an export sector with its own lighter rules beside a home market the state kept closed. In the 1990s and 2000s that export sector drew most private money and new jobs, mostly along the coast, and the economy was widely praised. The World Bank later wrote that the praise hid barriers to entry and privileges that held most firms back.

threads.title: Revolution without economic change
threads.text: Too few good jobs for graduates and wide gaps between regions fed the January 2011 revolution. Politics changed, but three years later the World Bank found the old economic system largely in place. Income per person fell 3.1 percent in 2011 and by 2019 was only modestly above its 2010 level.

threads.title: The pandemic blow
threads.text: In 2020 income per person fell 9.7 percent, its largest fall since 1963. The IMF said the pandemic made older weaknesses in the budget and in the balance with the rest of the world worse. Income per person rose 4.1 percent in 2021 but had not regained its 2019 peak by 2025.

threads.title: Debt and borrowing at home
threads.text: Public debt has stayed high and access to foreign markets limited, so the government has leaned on local banks and the central bank to fund its deficits. The World Bank says this has probably squeezed lending to private firms: credit to private firms fell from 67.7 percent of GDP in 2020 to 57.7 in 2025.

threads.title: A state-heavy economy, low investment
threads.text: Investment fell from 26.0 percent of GDP in 2010 to 15.2 percent in 2024. Recent reports describe state-owned firms that dominate key sectors, a state that became the employer of last resort as private hiring stalled, and weak investment and productivity.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 1.9 percent in 2025, up from 1.0 in 2024, as farm output recovered and construction and tourism picked up. In 2026 the conflict in the Middle East raised the energy import bill and widened the external gap, and repaying a maturing foreign bond in July drew reserves down sharply.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Tunisia, October 2026

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Tunisia, October 2026
citations.quote: Pressure on foreign reserves intensified in mid-July 2026, when reserves fell by 2.47 billion Tunisian dinars in a single day to repay a 2019 Eurobond.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a recovery in which total output finally passed its pre-pandemic level in 2025, but income per person in 2025 was still 1.7 percent below its 2019 peak. The World Bank itself notes why: since 2019 output has grown by about as much as the population.
